summaries.gardner: Goldman Sachs is a famous, top-dog brand in investment banking, but it is a mature, cyclical industry leader rather than a Rule Breaker in an emerging market. Its management is strong and it is backed by heavy institutional ownership, yet it lacks a fast-growing new market and the stock is not commonly called overvalued.
summaries.buffett: Goldman fits parts of Buffett's approach: a strong franchise, shrinking share count (317.6M diluted shares in 2025 vs 360.3M in 2020) and a price near 12-13 times earnings; Berkshire itself invested in Goldman in 2008 but later sold. Against it, earnings are cyclical, returns rely on about 16x balance-sheet leverage, and the business is hard to predict, which Buffett has cited as reasons to avoid investment banks.
summaries.munger: Munger valued quality franchises and avoided complexity and leverage; Goldman has the franchise but its trading book, $2.1 trillion balance sheet and dependence on markets make it a business with many ways to go wrong. It is a well-run firm in an industry Munger often criticised for incentives and opacity.
summaries.lynch: Goldman fits Lynch's cyclical category: earnings swing with deal and trading activity (EPS $22.87 in 2023 to $51.32 in 2025 and $55.56 for nine months of 2026). With a P/E of about 12.6 on trailing EPS and buybacks cutting the share count, the story is about where the capital-markets cycle stands, which Lynch would tell investors to watch closely.
summaries.fisher: Fisher looked for sustained sales growth from new products and outstanding management; Goldman has deep management and superb selling ability, but its revenue growth is cyclical (net revenues fell in 2022 and 2023) and it does not run R&D in the sense Fisher meant. Its failed consumer push shows new lines do not always succeed.
summaries.graham: Goldman passes Graham's size, profitability (profitable every year) and dividend-record tests, and EPS has grown far more than a third over ten years. It fails his price tests: the stock trades at about 23 times three-year average EPS and price/earnings times price/book is about 30, above Graham's 22.5 ceiling, and a broker-dealer's leverage is far from his defensive ideal.
summaries.thiel: Goldman is not a Zero to One business: it has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals and competes in a crowded oligopoly. It does score on distribution, a durable brand and an excellent team, but not on monopoly-like uniqueness or a secret others miss.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner favours companies riding big technology shifts with improving unit economics; Goldman is a cyclical bank that benefits from AI-driven capital raising and M&A but is not itself an AI platform. Its strong 2026 earnings rebound and buybacks would interest him, but growth beyond the cycle is modest.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on liquidity, rates and earnings momentum; Goldman's earnings were accelerating in 2026 (Q3 EPS $17.01 vs about $13.02 expected) but the stock fell about 24% from its July high near $1,154 as rate-hike worries and softer deal fees weighed. It is a macro-sensitive trade rather than a high-conviction long-term position.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids banks because they need leverage and earn low returns on capital, and Goldman's 15.0% ROE in 2025 came with liabilities about 16 times equity. It does not fit his 'good companies' test of high unlevered returns, steady growth and strong free cash flow.
summaries.greenblatt: The Magic Formula excludes financial companies, so Goldman cannot be ranked on earnings yield and return on capital in the usual way. Its earnings yield on price (about 7.9% at a 12.6x P/E) is decent, but return on capital without leverage is low.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs an extraordinary business, talented and honest managers, and great reinvestment opportunities; Goldman has capable management and a strong franchise but reinvests at bank-like returns and pays out much of its profit through buybacks and dividends. It is only a partial fit.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for simple businesses bought at a deep discount with low downside; Goldman is complex, leveraged and priced at about 2.4 times book value, so it offers no Dhandho-style 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' bet today.
summaries.wood: Goldman is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's sense: it is an incumbent financial institution, not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or sequencing. It uses these technologies internally but its addressable market will not multiply in five years.
summaries.ackman: Ackman wants simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and low leverage; Goldman has a dominant advisory franchise but is cyclical, highly leveraged and hard to predict. It fits his quality-franchise interest only partly.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep sought scale-economics-shared businesses that pass savings to customers; Goldman keeps its scale benefits as profit and pays top compensation, so it does not fit his model. Its 10-20 year position will likely be similar, not clearly stronger.
summaries.valentine: Don Valentine backed startups attacking huge new markets with technology; Goldman is a 157-year-old incumbent, so his venture framework does not really apply. It does serve a large market and solves real problems for big corporate clients.
summaries.nash: Goldman fails several of Nash's hard filters: more debt than cash, negative free cash flow, revenue growth below 10% in 2025 (8.9%) and liabilities about 16 times equity, and it scores about 65 of 130 on his categories. Its strengths are a strong earnings-beat record in 2026, low short interest and a forward P/E of about 12.5, but as a bank it is outside his preferred profile.

momentum.evidence: GS closed at $878.72 on October 14, 2026, up about 11.7% over 52 weeks but roughly 24% below its July 2026 high near $1,154, after falling from about $1,038 in early September.

g4.evidence: CEO David Solomon and President John Waldron (a planned successor) lead a deep partnership bench, and institutions own about 72% of the shares.

g6.evidence: At about 12.6 times trailing EPS ($69.57) and 2.4 times book value ($372.64), Goldman is not commonly called overvalued; the S&P Global consensus is Hold with a $1,054 average target.

simple.evidence: The business lines (advice, trading, asset management) are understandable, but a $2.1 trillion balance sheet with derivatives and trading risks is hard for a generalist to analyse well.

b2.evidence: Goldman has been profitable every year, but results swing widely: net earnings were $21.6B in 2021, $8.5B in 2023 and $17.2B in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Goldman returns capital rationally (2025 buybacks of $12.36B and a dividend raised to $5.00 a quarter), but $80M retention awards to Solomon and Waldron in 2025 drew shareholder criticism and the 1MDB scandal cost it billions.

b6.evidence: Goldman retreated from its consumer-banking push (Apple Card moving to Chase, announced January 7, 2026), but that venture itself was an expansion beyond its core and it continues bolt-on asset-management deals.

roic.evidence: ROE was 23.0% in 2021, 7.5% in 2023 and 15.0% in 2025, achieved with total liabilities of about 16 times shareholders' equity, so returns are neither consistent nor debt-free.

fcf.evidence: As a broker-dealer its operating cash flow swings with trading balances; net cash used for operating activities was $25.8B in the first half of 2026, so free cash flow does not track profit.

b10.evidence: Book value per share rose to $372.64 at September 30, 2026 and the share count fell from 360.3M (2020) to 301.1M (Q3 2026) while the market value is about 2.4 times book.

safety.evidence: At about 2.4 times book value and 12.6 times trailing EPS boosted by a strong 2026, the price does not offer a clear margin of safety against a conservative, through-cycle value.

fairprice.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 12.6 and forward P/E of about 12.5 is reasonable for a top franchise, but earnings are near cyclical highs (nine-month 2026 ROE 20.7%).

mu5.evidence: Goldman is well capitalised (CET1 12.4% standardized at September 2026) but, as a leveraged trading institution, it could be hurt by market shocks, legal events or funding stress.

reinvest.evidence: Goldman can deploy capital into private credit and wealth management, but it returns most earnings (2025 buybacks $12.36B and dividends $4.42B vs $16.3B net earnings to common), showing limited high-return reinvestment.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic cyclical: EPS dropped from $59.45 in 2021 to $22.87 in 2023 and recovered to $51.32 in 2025 as deal and trading activity rebounded.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 12.6 is below 2025 EPS growth of about 27% ($40.54 to $51.32), but consensus sees 2027 EPS ($72.74) only about 2% above 2026 ($70.97).

runway.evidence: Wealth and alternatives can keep growing (assets under supervision $4.1 trillion, up from $3.6 trillion at end-2025), but banking and trading revenue grows only with the cycle; net revenues grew about 5.5% a year in 2020-2025.

ly7.evidence: The company is shrinking its share count (diluted shares 317.6M in 2025 to 301.1M in Q3 2026, with $3.0B repurchased in Q3), but insiders are not open-market buyers.

ly8.evidence: Goldman is one of the most closely followed stocks on Wall Street, covered by about 25 analysts in the S&P Global consensus.

fi2.evidence: Management has built new growth lines in private credit, alternatives and wealth management, though its large consumer-banking effort was abandoned.

fi3.evidence: Goldman does not report R&D spending; its technology investment supports trading and platforms but its payoff cannot be measured separately.

fi4.evidence: Its client franchise is exceptional at winning mandates: No. 1 in 2025 global M&A, advising on $1.48 trillion of deals and 38 of 68 deals over $10B (LSEG).

longterm.evidence: Management invested for years in durable asset and wealth fees, but compensation and capital decisions remain tied closely to annual ROE targets.

gr1.evidence: Goldman had $58.3B of 2025 net revenues, about $2.1 trillion of assets and a market value of about $266B.

ni10.evidence: Goldman has been profitable every year in the last decade, including $8.5B of net earnings in its weak 2023 and $17.2B in 2025.

gr4.evidence: Goldman has paid a quarterly dividend every year since its 1999 IPO, more than 25 years, and raised it to $5.00 a quarter in 2026.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS more than doubled even over five years, from $24.74 in 2020 to $51.32 in 2025, far above the one-third growth threshold.

gr6.evidence: At $878.72 the price is about 23 times the 2023-2025 average diluted EPS of $38.24.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 12.6 (trailing $69.57 EPS) times P/B of about 2.36 ($372.64 book value) is about 29.8, above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Goldman's trading and risk platforms are strong but not ten times better than JPMorgan's or Morgan Stanley's.

timing.evidence: 2026 brought a strong deal and trading recovery (record Q2 net revenues of $20.3B), but rising rates and softer Q3 deal fees industry-wide hit the stock from July.

th3.evidence: Goldman is a 157-year-old incumbent in a large, mature market, not a company that started with a dominant share of a small niche.

team.evidence: Solomon, Waldron and a deep partner bench run a firm that ranked No. 1 in 2025 M&A and earned an annualised 20.7% ROE in the first nine months of 2026.

th5.evidence: Its senior-banker coverage of the world's largest companies, governments and investors is a powerful distribution channel built over decades.

durable.evidence: Its advisory brand should last, but electronic market makers, private credit funds and JPMorgan's balance sheet are eroding parts of its trading and lending franchise.

th7.evidence: Its strategy of shifting toward wealth, alternatives and private credit is the same one Morgan Stanley and others pursue.

trend.evidence: Goldman benefits from AI-driven capital raising, private markets growth and rising wealth, but as an adviser and intermediary rather than a direct platform.

dr1.evidence: Earnings accelerated in 2026 (nine-month EPS $55.56 vs $51.32 for all of 2025), but analysts made 17 downward Q3 EPS revisions in the 30 days before the October 13 report, and 2027 consensus EPS is barely above 2026.

dr2.evidence: Outcomes depend on the deal cycle, rates and the possible Waldron succession, none of which clearly favour a better picture in 18-24 months than consensus already expects.

dr4.evidence: Buoyant markets and M&A helped 2026, but rising Treasury yields and rate-hike worries in September-October 2026 pressured capital-markets activity and the stock.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include a pickup in mega-deal M&A and IPOs, the finished Apple Card exit (about 24 months from January 2026), lighter capital rules and continued buybacks.

dr7.evidence: Cyclical earnings and high leverage make it unsuitable for a large, concentrated position for most investors.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is not meaningful for a bank; its pre-tax margin was 37.5% in 2025.

fcfyield.evidence: Free cash flow is negative and volatile for a broker-dealer (StockAnalysis shows about -$41.5B trailing), so free-cash-flow yield is not a useful or attractive measure.

gb2.evidence: Enterprise value is not meaningful for a bank whose borrowings are operating liabilities, so operating profit to EV cannot be judged fairly.

pa2.evidence: The stock's roughly 24% fall from its July 2026 high reflects rate fears and softer deal fees, which look temporary, but the business itself delivered a Q3 2026 earnings beat.

pa4.evidence: Strong capital (CET1 12.4%) and a top franchise limit permanent-loss risk, but leverage and market exposure leave real tail risks.

wo1.evidence: Goldman is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing, though it uses AI internally.

wo2.evidence: Its costs do not fall rapidly with volume; operating expenses rose 11.2% in 2025 to $37.5B as net revenues rose 8.9%.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several disruptive innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market of capital markets and wealth grows with the economy, not many times over in five years.

ac3.evidence: Its results depend heavily on interest rates, market volatility and deal activity, as shown by net revenues falling to $46.3B in 2023.

ns1.evidence: Goldman keeps scale benefits as profit and pays high compensation rather than passing savings to clients.

ns4.evidence: Growing wealth and alternatives fees may make it steadier in 10-20 years, but competition from JPMorgan and nonbanks makes a clearly stronger position uncertain.

va2.evidence: It solves big problems for companies and investors: raising capital, completing mergers and managing risk on deals worth trillions.

tn1.evidence: Goldman is a long-established bank, not a company built for a secular trend such as AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market still prices Goldman as a volatile trading house, while about 29% of 2025 net revenues came from asset and wealth management and AUS passed $4 trillion.

tn3.evidence: Goldman is a large-cap US company (about $266B market value) and not in any of Nash's avoid zones.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable ($17.2B 2025 net earnings) and revenue grew in 2024 and 2025, but it has more debt than cash ($437.9B unsecured borrowings vs $187.3B cash at June 2026), as is normal for a bank.

tn7.evidence: Free cash flow is negative, so revenue growth plus FCF margin falls well short of 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 net revenues grew 8.9% while total operating expenses grew 11.2% ($33.8B to $37.5B).

tn9.evidence: It trips Nash's instant kill of more debt than cash ($437.9B of unsecured borrowings vs $187.3B cash), though its pre-tax margin (37.5%), market cap and founding date pass.

tn10.evidence: No existential legal threat is pending, but Goldman faces constant regulatory scrutiny, capital-rule changes and litigation, as the 1MDB settlement showed.

tn11.evidence: Goldman provides advice, financing, trading and asset management that help companies, governments and investors raise capital, complete deals and grow wealth, charging advisory and underwriting fees, trading spreads and asset-based management fees.

tn13.evidence: Total about 65: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 5 (about 20% TTM), operating margin 10, short interest 10 (2.3%), institutional ownership 10 (72%), revenue vs expenses 0, 5-year return vs S&P 5, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 0, secular trend 0, culture 5, talent 10.

tn15.evidence: Total liabilities of $2.0 trillion are about 16 times the $122.7B of shareholders' equity at June 30, 2026, far above Nash's 4x limit, as is typical for a broker-dealer bank.

tn18.evidence: Solomon has run Goldman since October 2018 with record 2025-2026 results, but he is not a founder, has under 10 years as CEO and is not an open-market buyer of shares.

tn20.evidence: Goldman beat consensus EPS in the last four quarters, including Q1 2026 ($17.55 vs $16.99), Q2 2026 ($20.98 vs about $14.50) and Q3 2026 ($17.01 vs $13.02 LSEG consensus).

tn21.evidence: No accounting or fraud concerns, but margins fell sharply in 2022-2023, there is an active CEO succession debate and executives such as Solomon sell stock rather than buy.

tn22.evidence: Goldman has large revenues ($58.3B in 2025), is profitable and is shrinking its share count rather than issuing shares.

tn24.evidence: At about 12.6 times trailing EPS the price implies low growth, roughly in line with or below the 2026 recovery, but trailing earnings are near a cyclical peak.

tn25.evidence: Nash's DCF cannot support today's price because Goldman's free cash flow is negative and borrowings exceed cash.
